input.text: If you are an American bullfrog, you start to avoid a looming object when it spans about 20 degrees of what you see, which is about ten human thumbs held at arm's length. If you are a European toad, nerve cells that signal a moving object can be suppressed when a black-and-white textured background moves at the same speed, and if you are a cane toad, a review of prey-catching tests states that you strike at a moving insect-like model. Nobody has measured how you see motion in most other frogs and toads, including the American toad.
input.note: Replaced "reports" with "states" because the voice check bans it. Left out R3 (Japanese toad) and R5 (Guayaquil dwarf frog) for length.

input.text: A human reads about 30 cycles a degree on an eye chart, and the few insects measured see far less fine detail than that. If you are a common green darner you see about a fifteenth as much as a human, and if you are an orange sulphur about a fortieth. If you are an Old World swallowtail, a table compiled from the literature gives about a fiftieth, and for most other insects nobody has measured how sharply you see.
input.note: Gave sharpness as fractions of a human's 30 cycles a degree instead of decimals; left out the facet-angle figures and the other measured species.

input.text: A review lists two kinds of color-sensing cell in cattle, sheep, goats and horses, where a human has three, and you very likely have two as well. Measurements in the white-tailed deer found a cell most sensitive to blue, and measurements in the fallow deer found one most sensitive to green.
input.note: Replaced "reports" with "lists". R6 only states cones and rods, so it is not cited for a cone count. I left out wavelength figures because they have no comparison job.

input.text: If you are a white-tailed deer, you see a fifth or less of the fine detail a human sees, and a light-reflecting layer called the tapetum lucidum covers the upper part of your eye and overlaps the horizontal strip where you see most sharply. A review of deer eyes states that deer in general have this layer, so other deer very likely have it too. Nobody has measured how dim a light you can see by, and nobody has tested how you judge depth.
input.note: Dim-light sensitivity and depth cue have no deer records (only horse, sheep, cattle), so both are stated as unmeasured. Replaced "reports" with "states" for the voice check.

input.text: For most birds, nobody has measured how sharply you see. If you are a house sparrow, you read about 5 cycles a degree, and if you are a mallard, about 12 (an estimate from the density of cells in the retina), where a human reads about 30 on an eye chart. If you are a Eurasian magpie or a western jackdaw, a compilation of behavior tests gives about 30, close to a human.
input.note: No record for spacing of light-sensing cells (interreceptor_deg), so it is left out; figures stay with the species named.

input.text: In the honey bee, three kinds of color-sensing cell have been measured, peaking in ultraviolet, blue and green, and a review reports the same three kinds in the buff-tailed bumblebee, the large red-tailed bumblebee and the European wool carder bee. None of the three kinds peaks in red, even in the large red-tailed bumblebee. If you are another bee, you very likely have these same three kinds.
input.note: No record says how red things look to a bee, so I left out the "look dark" claim from the example row.

input.text: Your eyesight is much blurrier than a human's. If you are a domestic dog, a review cites an estimate of 20/75 for a typical dog, which means you must stand 20 feet from what a human can make out from 75 feet. If you are a red fox, the cells in your retina allow about 6 cycles a degree, a fifth of a human's 30, and if you are an arctic fox the estimate is about 9.
input.note: Left out coyotes, wolves, jackals and other foxes (carried grade g) and the unmeasured species to stay within three sentences.

input.text: Your eyes sit on the sides of your head, and a book on deer says they let you watch almost a complete circle, about 310 degrees. The book does not say how that was found, and nobody has measured how much of the space around you both of your eyes see at once. In goats, which are not deer, a review states a field of 320 to 340 degrees, with 20 to 60 degrees seen by both eyes together.
input.note: No deer record measures field or binocular overlap; R10 is a book statement with no stated method, so it is attributed to the book. Goat figures are named as goat figures only.

input.text: If you are a cane toad, a review of flicker measurements lists 7 flashes a second as the speed at which a light starts to look steady to you, the lowest value in its table. A human stops seeing flicker at about 60 flashes a second. Nobody has measured how fast a flicker you can see if you are any other frog or toad, so nobody can say whether you are as slow as the cane toad.
input.note: Only the cane toad has a figure, read from a review table; I did not carry it to other Rhinella toads. Replaced "reports" with "lists" to pass the voice check.

input.text: If you are a chicory, your flower heads open in the early morning and fade as daylight reaches its greatest intensity. If you are a black locust, a review found that your leaflets move by day and by night, and that they stand more upright in stronger light. For most other plants, nobody has measured how you sense light or how you keep track of the time of day.
input.note: No record covers green light specifically, so the row does not mention green. Replaced "reports" with "found" to pass the voice check.

input.text: If you are a heron, egret or crane, nobody has measured how sharply you see, or how closely spaced the light-sensing cells in your eye are. Two doves have a figure: a compilation lists a rock pigeon at about 12 cycles a degree in behavior tests, and a table lists a mourning dove at about 7, estimated from cell counts in its retina. A human reads about 30 cycles a degree, and those two figures belong to those two doves alone.
input.note: Replaced "reports" with "lists". No record gives acuity or receptor spacing for any heron, egret or crane, so the row stays at i.

input.text: If you are a domestic dog, a review estimates that you take in about 240 degrees around you, where a human takes in 180, and that your two eyes overlap by 30 to 60 degrees. In dim light you have more rods than a human, even in the center of the retina where a human has none, and about 7 in 10 dogs examined had a full-sized tapetum, the mirror layer behind the retina, while a few had none. Nobody has measured how well you judge depth.
input.note: Dropped the 539 count and the 2 percent figure. The depth sentence rests on no record, because R5 is a cat record on focusing range.

input.text: If you are a red-tailed hawk, a compilation of measurements puts you at about 17 cycles a degree, where a human reads about 30 on an eye chart. A black kite in that compilation reads about 35, and the eagle Aquila audax up to 140. Nobody has measured how sharply you see if you are a bald eagle, an osprey or most other species in your group.
input.note: Rounded 33 to 35 and 138 to 140. Left out the 160 book figure (R13) because it names no species, and left out interreceptor_deg because no record has it.

input.text: If you are a pond slider, you have four kinds of color-sensing cone, one of them for ultraviolet, and a review estimates from the cells in your retina that you see about a fifth of the detail a human sees. Sharpness has been measured in only a few other species, including the green anole, the brown anole, the box turtle and the common watersnake, and nobody has measured it in most lizards, snakes and turtles. Nobody has measured how far around you can see, and pupil shape is known for only a few species, such as the round pupils of the painted turtle and the garter snake.
input.note: Replaced "reports" with "estimates". No record gives field of view for any reptile, so the row says so. The ultraviolet cone is stated only for the pond slider.

input.text: If you are a European rabbit, you can see all the way around you when you crouch in the freeze position, and only about 25 degrees straight ahead is seen by both eyes. You have round pupils, two kinds of color-sensing cell (blue and green), and about a tenth of the fine detail a human sees, and a review states that you have no tapetum, the reflective layer behind the retina. Nobody has measured any of this in cottontails, hares or pikas, so if you are one of those, how your eyes work is unknown.
input.note: Left out R9 and the Iberian rabbit carry, since fields travel only within a genus; peak wavelengths dropped as they had no job.

input.text: If you are a gray squirrel, a fox squirrel or a Eurasian red squirrel, nobody has measured how fast a flicker your eyes can follow. Among relatives, a compilation of measurements lists American red squirrels at about 60 flashes a second, the same as a human, and golden-mantled ground squirrels at more than 100. The southern flying squirrel follows flicker only up to about 10 to 15 flashes a second.
input.note: No cff_hz record exists for Sciurus, so the row stays at i. I removed "active at night" for the flying squirrel because no record states it.

input.text: If you are a gray heron, little egret, intermediate egret, Pacific reef heron or tick bird, your head most often bobs once for each step you take, as filmed in wild birds. If you are a black-crowned night heron, you see about 320 degrees around you at once. Nobody has measured either one in a great blue heron, a great egret or a green heron.
input.note: Changed "grey" to "gray". Left out pigeon, moorhen and squacco figures; the Ardeidae 170 degree field (R30) is for one eye only.

input.text: In an eyetracker study of jumping spiders, the retinas inside the two big front eyes moved, and the spiders spent more time looking at still or slowly moving images. If you are a bold jumping spider, your front eyes need guidance from the pair of eyes beside them to find and follow a moving object, but they scan a still shape without that guidance. Nobody has measured the eye movements of most other jumping spiders, so how your own retinas move is unknown.
input.note: Left out the fovea: R5's quote does not state the receptor density figure, and R3 covers only Lyssomanes. R2 (Marpissa marina priming) left out for length.

input.text: If you are an American alligator, the dark opening in the middle of each eye is a vertical slit. If you are a China alligator, you very likely have the same, since your close relative the American alligator does. Among crocodiles, the saltwater crocodile has a vertical, mobile slit pupil, and nobody has measured the pupil shape of the other crocodiles, the caimans or the gharial.
input.note: Removed the word "report". Caiman, gharial and most crocodile species have no pupil record, so the row says nobody has measured them.

input.text: If you are a wood strawberry, you sense red and far-red light with a protein called phytochrome B, and according to a review, your daughter plants grow more root over live ground than over dead ground. If you are a common selfheal, a review found that strong far-red light slowed the growth of your plantlets in a lab. For most of you, nobody has measured whether you sense a neighbor by its light or by its scent.
input.note: Replaced "reports" with "according to a review" and "a review found". Left out the dandelion: R1 gives no result. No record says neighbors change the light a plant gets, so the row does not say that.

input.text: Nobody has measured how sharply most of you see, only how closely your light-sensing cells sit. If you are a bold jumping spider, the cells in the sharpest zone of your side eyes sit about half a degree apart. In the big front eyes of Phidippus johnsoni, a relative, they sit about 9 minutes of arc apart, which is much less than a degree.
input.note: Removed the 60 minutes per degree figure, which no record states. Left out R3 because its quote gives only a visual angle, and R5 to avoid decimals.

input.text: Your pupil is a slit lying on its side, wider than it is tall. It has been recorded this way in white-tailed deer, red deer, moose, reindeer, pudu and gray brocket. If you are a reindeer, the slit measures about 25 square millimeters when narrowed, and the pupil opens to a round shape of about 335 square millimeters when dilated.
input.note: Removed the "13 times larger" figure, which was my own division and not in a record. No record gives the pupil of mule deer, roe deer or fallow deer, so the row names only the measured deer.

input.text: A review lists a rock pigeon seeing a light flicker at about 75 flashes a second and a chicken at about 85, where a human stops seeing flicker at about 60. If you are a heron, egret, crane or another wading bird, nobody has measured how fast a light can flash before you stop seeing the flicker.
input.note: No record covers herons, egrets, cranes or other waders; only rock pigeon (75 Hz) and chicken (87 Hz) are measured, both read from a review (Boström 2016). Replaced "reports" with "lists" and dropped the unsupported ground-feeding remark.

input.text: Ultraviolet is light that humans cannot see at all. In the blue tit, the European starling and the Eurasian blackbird, one kind of color-sensing cell peaks in it, between 360 and 375 nanometers, and a review table gives 315 nanometers as the point where the blue tit's lens and cornea pass half the light, so if you are a songbird you very likely sense ultraviolet. If you are a mallard, the matching cell peaks at 415 nanometers, in violet, and if you are a cormorant you very likely get almost no ultraviolet, since the lens and cornea of the pied cormorant block it.
input.note: Replaced "reports" with "a review table gives". Left out the house sparrow (R13 is not its ultraviolet cell), the goldfinch's 399 nm and the great cormorant's 405 nm cell to keep the row short.
